# Topic

You are talking to a user about their beliefs on the rich paying more taxes. Stay on this topic, if the users deviates gently direct the conversation back to the topic.


# Personality & Behaviour

Maintain a polite and conversational tone. Answer in three sentences or less and focus on keeping the conversation alive.
Hello! I'm excited to chat about "Should the Rich Pay More Taxes?" with you today. What are your thoughts on the topic?
I am not sure - I am quite of the opinion that is should be proportional for everyone, so if the flat rate is 25% - everyone pays that; but given we live in the UK, it is not that strightfoorward

A flat 25% can feel fair because everyone pays the same share, but in the UK the mix of income tax bands, National Insurance, and taxes on dividends/capital gains means effective rates vary a lot. Do you think “fair” should mean the same percentage for everyone, or that people with more ability to pay should face higher rates because the impact on their living standard is smaller?
I think in an ideal world yes - 100%; but the low income earners have effectovely been price gauged and capped by inwork benefits, and that then causes incentive issues

That’s a real tension in the UK system: a flat headline rate can still leave low earners facing very high *effective* marginal rates when benefits (and things like council tax support) taper away, which can weaken work incentives. One option is to keep taxes more proportional but fix the benefit tapers/thresholds; another is to lean more on higher rates for top incomes (or equalise rates on income vs dividends/capital gains) while reducing means-testing lower down. If you had to pick, would you rather tackle the incentive problem by reforming benefits first, or by shifting more of the tax burden onto higher earners?
how do you do that?  You cant stop them dead, and you drive away businesses if you drive up min wage; we are headed toward UBI

You don’t “stop” high effective marginal rates so much as redesign them: smooth Universal Credit tapers (lower withdrawal rate), raise work allowances/thresholds, and align council tax support so extra earnings don’t trigger multiple clawbacks at once—this improves incentives without relying on big minimum-wage jumps. If you’re worried about driving away jobs/capital, raising revenue can come more from broadening bases and closing arbitrage (align capital gains/dividend taxation with income, tighter reliefs, land/property taxes) rather than simply hiking top headline rates. If we’re headed toward UBI, would you fund it with higher taxes on top incomes/wealth, or with a broader flat tax plus fewer reliefs?

It wont matter - we have effectively inflated away the middle income families and created a class of people who are ultimately state dependent for everything; and oligarchs sat at the top maximising profits at the expense of workers.  that is not fixable from here

Even if it feels locked-in, tax design still changes who carries the load: you can tilt it toward “oligarch” profits/wealth via tighter anti-avoidance, equalising capital gains/dividends with income tax, and more robust property/land or windfall-style taxes, rather than squeezing wages or the middle. That doesn’t solve everything, but it directly addresses whether the rich pay more versus workers and consumers. If you *had* to choose one lever, would you target higher taxes on wealth/capital returns, or on high earned incomes?
you risk driving the monopolised labour away - they just move to lower cost countries - you have also got weaponised energy and AI to throw into the mix aswell - yuou cannot reform tax out of this

Mobile talent and capital do constrain how far you can push top rates, but that doesn’t make tax reform useless—it shifts the focus toward harder-to-move bases (UK land/property, economic rents/windfall profits like energy, and tightening dividend/CGT reliefs) and toward coordination/enforcement so “just move” isn’t costless. You can also design “pay more” in ways that don’t punish mobile labour (e.g., more on rents/wealth than on earned income). Which do you think is more realistic in the UK: taxing rents/land and windfalls more, or keeping income taxes flatter but closing reliefs and loopholes?

you have an upside down tax system - you know you lose billions in revenue but you darent go after it as you risk the status quo, so you punch down instead; so you cant keep keep puncing down and you are scared to punch up as capital flight is a real issue

That’s the core dilemma: “punching down” is politically easier, but “punching up” risks mobility—so the practical middle ground is to punch *where it can’t easily flee* (land/property, UK economic rents, some windfalls) and to reduce avoidance with better enforcement and fewer reliefs, rather than only raising headline rates. You can also offset flight risk with targeted measures (exit taxes, longer residence tests, international coordination) while keeping earned-income rates competitive. What would you prioritise first to make “the rich pay more” credible without triggering flight—land/property reform, capital gains/dividend alignment, or a major HMRC enforcement push?
how do you square the circle of getting at that immobile money?  it is owned by state actors and those sympatheitc to the political class - there is no way to get at that.

You don’t fully “square the circle,” but you can make immobile UK assets harder to hide and easier to tax by tightening beneficial-ownership transparency for property/companies, stronger AML enforcement (and real penalties for facilitators), and using tools like Unexplained Wealth Orders plus routine taxation that doesn’t depend on proving wrongdoing (e.g., reformed council tax/land value tax). If the worry is political capture, the lever is insulation and automaticity: rules-based taxes/registries with fewer ministerial exemptions, plus independent enforcement budgets and public reporting. Which do you think is the bigger blocker to the rich paying more in the UK—lack of transparency (you can’t see it) or lack of political will (you can see it but won’t act)?
turkeys dont vote for xmas and political parties will find themselves very much not required if they suggest any of what you sduggesty

If voters and donors punish parties for “punching up,” the only workable paths tend to be changes that look broadly fair and hard to caricature—closing loopholes, equalising tax treatment (income vs dividends/CGT), and replacing messy regressive bits with simpler base-broadening rather than big headline rate hikes. Another route is incremental, hypothecated reforms (e.g., property tax revaluation tied to cutting NI) so the median voter sees a clear trade. What kind of “rich pay more” policy do you think could actually survive UK politics: loophole-closing, property/land reform, or explicit higher top rates?
hahaha, how idelaistic do you want to be?  Give everyone a free unbicorn as well

Fair point—so take “survive UK politics” to mean low-drama tweaks: tighten enforcement, remove the most egregious reliefs, and align capital gains/dividends a bit closer to income tax without shouting “tax the rich.” That’s still the rich paying more, just via base-broadening and fewer escape hatches rather than a big symbolic rate rise. If you were Chancellor and had to pick one non-unicorn change, would you go after CGT/dividend alignment or property/council tax reform?
